title: Our duty to praise
hook: once a High Holy Day prayer, now said at the end of every service

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mi Sheberach, the blessing for the sick, the community and the country. Your line was pray for the city. Today, the prayer that closes almost every service.

Morning, afternoon or evening, the last few minutes of a synagogue service tend to sound alike. People stand. The tune picks up. And at one line, the room bends its knees and bows, together. It sounds like an ending that was always there. Historians say otherwise. For a long stretch, this prayer belonged to Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, in the solemn season of the High Holy Days. Then, sometime in the Middle Ages, it moved out of the High Holy Days and into every single day.
screen: `THE WHOLE ROOM BOWS.` → `ONCE A NEW YEAR PRAYER.` → `NOW EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Its first word is aleinu: it is upon us, it is our duty. The opening says, roughly, it is our duty to praise the Master of all, to give greatness to the one who formed the world. Then the bowing line: and we bend the knee and bow and give thanks before the King of kings. That's when people bow. Where did it come from? Tradition credits Joshua. Some scholars connect it with the sage Rav in Babylonia, who is said to have arranged the Rosh Hashanah prayers about God's kingship; Aleinu opens that section. On the High Holy Days it keeps its old drama: in many synagogues the cantor, and sometimes everyone, kneels and lowers all the way to the floor, a posture the rest of the year's prayers don't ask for. The second paragraph turns outward, toward a hope: a day when the world will be repaired under the kingship of God. The Hebrew phrase there, l'taken olam, to repair the world, is one of the roots of the modern words tikkun olam. It ends with a verse from Zechariah, in the old Jewish translation: "And the LORD shall be King over all the earth; in that day shall the LORD be One, and His name one." So the prayer moves in two steps: our duty to praise, right now, on our knees, and the hope that one day the whole world will join in. The service ends holding both.
screen: `ALEINU: IT IS UPON US.` · `WE BEND THE KNEE AND BOW.` · `FROM ROSH HASHANAH TO EVERY DAY.` · `TO REPAIR THE WORLD.` · then, large: `OUR DUTY TO PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, and if you pray, say the opening in your own language: it is our duty to praise. At we bend the knee and bow, do just that, knees soft, a bow from the waist, then come back up slowly and stand a moment, letting your body remember what it just said.
Aleinu. It is upon us. The prayer of duty and hope that closes the service, with a bow in the middle.
Your line: bow now, and hope later. A week of Tachanun, the ark opening, the yad, lifting the scroll, the haftarah, Mi Sheberach and Aleinu. That's day six hundred two.

howItsDone: Aleinu is said standing at the end of the morning, afternoon and evening services, and many people bend the knees and bow at the line about bending the knee; on the High Holy Days many congregations kneel and prostrate fully during it.

chat.says: Why does everyone bow in the middle of that last prayer at services?
options: It's the line we bend the knee and bow, before the King of kings.
It's when the leader finishes, so everyone bows to thank the leader.
It's when the mourners stand up, so the whole room bows to honor them.
chat.meaning: Aleinu says we bend the knee and bow and give thanks before the King of kings, and at that line the room does it.

notes: Zechariah 14:9 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Attribution: tradition credits Joshua; many scholars link it to Rav (3rd century) and the Rosh Hashanah Malchuyot. Confirm wording.
Aleinu entered the daily service in medieval Ashkenaz (often dated to the 12th–14th centuries); left vague as 'sometime in the Middle Ages'.
Full prostration on the High Holy Days: practice varies (cantor only in some congregations, everyone in others).
The bowing line echoes Isaiah 45:23; paraphrased, not quoted.
The medieval censorship of a line of Aleinu is deliberately omitted.
